items.question: How do you think about pursuing partnerships with companies that could compete with you on Spark products?
items.object: Partnerships with companies that could compete on Spark products
items.answer: We are going to be aggressive also about partnerships, even though the partners could compete and overlap, because you have to trust yourself that at least when it comes to Spark, you can build the best products. We are kind of saying internally, well, if someone else is building a better product for Spark then we deserve to lose, right? So that was always the confidence, that we can build the best product for Spark, and eventually, if Spark wins, we are going to win.

items.question: How do you see Databricks’ current focus on AI fitting into your original vision for the company?
items.object: Databricks’ platform vision and its current focus on AI
items.answer: I think with Databricks, we always wanted to provide the platform, an entire platform, which helps our customers get most of the value out of their data. One of the best ways today to get value out of the data is using these kinds of new developments in AI, including large language models and everything else. And the one thing to note is that this was always our vision from day one. Actually, Spark was created—one of the main reasons to create it, my take when we built it, was to solve, to speed up classical machine learning algorithms, right? And to scale them up. Right? And so, in some sense, for us it's full circle. We started this AI with machine learning, classic machine learning, and right now we are back and doing more and more AI to take advantage and create value out of the data.

items.question: What do you see as the main challenge in turning today’s AI capabilities into valuable products?
items.object: Turning AI capabilities into valuable production products
items.answer: I think that taking advantage and being successful with AI is not easy. The AI ecosystem is growing in complexity. It's not just a simple call to a model. You have so many techniques now like RAG and RAFT to improve the accuracy of your application using AI. Obviously, everyone is excited about AI because it solves so many problems and generates so many headlines. But still, it's not what you want. You want a product of AI. A lot of things still we're seeing today are fantastic demos. Demos are inspirational. And when people see demos, whatever ChatGPT solves, these kinds of problems, Olympics math problems, it's very easy to think that, wow, doing that, it's going to do everything. But going from demo to production, like I said, it's a big step. A demo means that you need to find an instance, at least an instance, to be really impressive. But when you go from the demo to the product, when you have a product, it has to work for all cases. So that's the big gap. That's why the effort is to improve accuracy, improve reliability, of course, eliminate hallucinations as much as you can, and really also to find where it provides the best value, because you can apply AI to 1,000 use cases, but which are the use cases which are going to provide you the biggest value? I think that's what we are also trying to help our customers with: to navigate how to successfully apply AI to their product, to improve their services, to their business.

items.question: Why did you see releasing DBRX as an open-source model as important for Databricks’ enterprise customers?
items.object: Databricks’ reasons for releasing DBRX as an open-source model
items.answer: So I think if you look at our main market, it's enterprise and enterprise customers. They do have a lot of concerns about data privacy, confidentiality, and obviously they kind of want control. It's not only that; they want auditability, right? They want to be able to audit what data you used, what results have been used, and what decisions have been made, with what data the decisions have been made. So we can host models on their machines or in their VPC and so forth. So it's one of the reasons for releasing DBRX, to help our customers. And then the customers, in many of these cases, they start from this model and then fine-tune with their own data to optimize for their particular use case, right? So again, our enterprise customers, they want, in the open-source models, control, as much visibility as they can. They want privacy and confidentiality, especially in the recent light of the breaches, which are widely published. The other thing is that the DNA of Databricks has been open source. It's not only Spark, but Delta and MLflow and many others.

items.question: Why do you consider programming copilots such an important use case for enterprises?
items.object: Programming copilots as an enterprise use case
items.answer: I think copilot programmability is one of the very important use cases in enterprises because software engineers are still very expensive. Making the people you have productive, and it's not only about that. Hiring top software engineering is very difficult, right? If you are a large company like maybe, I don't know, 4G or something like that. And so making those people productive is extremely important and critical for their business.

items.question: Why do you see open-source AI models as a compelling value proposition for enterprises?
items.object: Open-source AI models for enterprise use
items.answer: I think it's pre-training and then it's fine-tuning and using the model on your own hardware, in your own VPC, on your own machines. There are still a few doing pre-training once they have enough data. A lot of them want to do fine-tuning, right? Because look, if you are an enterprise, and a company, and you want to improve your business, what do you have and which others don't? The thing you have which others don't is the data. The data about your business, about your users. So, therefore, because this is something you have and others do not, you want to take advantage of that. So how do you take advantage of that? Again, there are many ways and you try different ways to do it. One is about fine-tuning user data and you have an open-source model, you fine-tune on that. The other one is to use RAG and something like that. And so you are going to do any of those, but then you want to do it in your own VPC, right? To preserve security, to have a security perimeter, you want to do it in order to protect confidentiality of your users. Obviously right now, with GDPR, the California Consumer Privacy Act and so forth, there are a lot of regulations. And the number of regulations is going to increase. So the fact that with open-source models you can fine-tune and you can use this RAG in your own VPC, it's a very compelling value proposition.

items.question: Under what conditions do you think enterprises will prefer open-source AI models over proprietary models from providers like OpenAI?
items.object: Enterprise adoption of open-source versus proprietary AI models
items.answer: I think enterprises—and we're still early on—and there are many enterprises obviously using OpenAI for different use cases, different applications. And I'm sure OpenAI and Microsoft Azure will come with new products to provide better confidentiality, better security. But at the end of the day, what I was saying is that, everything being equal, as an enterprise, I will prefer more control, security, and strategic, right? It's less kind of locking or something like that, right? So I think that's what we are saying. So if open-source models are going to catch up with the proprietary models, in particular in the use cases which matter for the enterprises, it doesn't need to be perfect for all the particular use cases. They just need to be very competitive where it matters. Then enterprises will prefer these solutions on which they have more control and more secure.

items.question: How do you assess whether open-source AI applications can outperform proprietary models like ChatGPT for particular use cases?
items.object: Open-source AI applications competing with proprietary models
items.answer: So, you have a lot of use cases. Again, it's the open source plus data. Right now the applications are more complex. It's not just a call to a large language model. You compose, you have applications which are built from many components. That's what they call compound AI. And so, actually, it turns out that if you can build applications for doing recommendation or something like that, or for programming for a particular compiler, for a particular tool, you can actually do better than even something like OpenAI on the latest ChatGPT because you have more data. And the other thing about Databricks, which I think there are also announcements about, is that with Unity Catalog and something like that, you have access and you know also about the structure of the data, which helps you tremendously to improve the accuracy of your applications. But I say it's not only the model, right? It's everything else you have around it and the quality of the data you feed it in. So I think that's—it's a data, stupid, like you say, right? Like at the end of the day.

items.question: How do you see enterprise priorities changing as an AI application moves from initial evaluation to deployment at scale?
items.object: Enterprise priorities when evaluating and scaling AI applications
items.answer: I think obviously cost is important. And it's like this, right? First of all, initially the important thing is about the value, right? Can you provide the value? That's the first thing. And at that stage, cost is not as important, right? In some of these early stages, people also try to use the most powerful model, like OpenAI and things like that. But once you cross that and you have a use case which you conclude is good at value to your business, now you want to scale it up, right? And now you are talking about having more control and more security and all of these things, protect confidentiality of the data, privacy of your users and so forth. And now basically people consider how they are going to deploy it. And this is where having multiple choices and having, like you said, more control, security, it matters. And where open-source models and platforms like Databricks are very valuable, right? And again, it's also all the other components which are together in Databricks, like I mentioned, like Unity Catalog and everything else to increase the value of your applications.

items.question: How do you think about the design of a compound AI system?
items.object: Compound AI systems
items.answer: A compound AI system basically consists of multiple components, multiple calls to large language models or agents. And you can think about it very much like when you write a program. You have multiple components. You have different function procedures to do different things, and then you put them together to create a program. The same is very similar here. You can use maybe one model to parse the data, to extract the data. Depending on the prompt, you may use a model if the prompt is about math problems. You can use one model. If the prompt is about programming, you may use a different model, right? And then you may use, for instance, for formatting the result, that's another one. Now more and more you are talking about agents, and with agents you have to call external services, functions like search, or you can use a calculator and things like that. So now you have different models. You can do a better job, and they are small models actually, to take the prompt and convert it to a function call. So that's kind of what it is. But the way I think about it conceptually is like you write a program, has different components, and make it easier to develop, deploy, and manage. The same thing you want to apply to AI applications.

items.question: How did you think about data scientists as the initial market for Databricks?
items.object: Data scientists as Databricks' initial target market
items.answer: When we started, indeed, we were focusing on building a product, a cloud product, hosted product for data scientists. We have this kind of notebook, and we provided hosted Spark, and we targeted data scientists. One of the reasons we targeted data scientists was because, again, we had Spark early on and also were targeting machine learning applications, machine learning workloads. At that time there were not many data scientists; it was 2013. However, when you look around, most of the universities already have data science programs and degrees. They were starting to offer data science degrees, and we were saying, okay, it seems a good path forward, a good market. I remember we were looking at LinkedIn to see how many data scientists there were, because our users initially weren't as many. Thousands, especially when you compare the data with database analysts and engineers and so forth.

items.question: What did you learn from early customers that shaped Databricks' expansion beyond its original data science focus?
items.object: Databricks' expansion from data science into data engineering and machine learning products
items.answer: I remember that we sold to these companies to use Databricks, and they were aspirationally buying it to do data science, AI. After a few months we would go to them, because we didn't go much earlier because we saw that they were doing well, their usage was growing, and everything seemed good. So no reason to worry. So we went back to them to see what they were doing. Maybe we can write a blog post or whatever they're doing, right? It's like marketing and everything. The surprise is that very few were actually doing machine learning at that time. And we asked them what happened. It turns out that in order to do machine learning, you need data, like we discussed earlier on. They realized that for the particular application they wanted, they don't have the data they need. So they need to add new logs, to collect new logs in their products and things like that. And also they need to clean up the data, curate the data and so forth. So we were lucky because Spark was very good also for data engineering, for data processing. It's a data processing tool at the end of the day. And so they were using Spark for data engineering. And then obviously we started focusing also on serving data engineers much more than before. And then later, now, we got the data engineering right, and still have all these data scientists exploring and starting to build models. Then it is a very natural extension to start to add more products for our users, for our customers, like I mentioned, to get more value out of their data. And that meant building machine learning models and using the open-source models.

items.question: How do you see the Microsoft partnership in the context of your broader partnership strategy at Databricks?
items.object: Databricks’ partnership strategy and its partnership with Microsoft
items.answer: Look, obviously the partnership with Microsoft was a great partnership for us. The one thing I want to say is that this is most visible. From day one, we were actually very focused on partnerships. Our idea was always, we make Spark successful, hopefully the de facto standard for data processing, and then we make Databricks the best place to run Spark. So early on, a few months into the life of the company, we had this kind of partnership with Cloudera. And then we had one with Hortonworks. This partnership was mainly because we were in the Hadoop ecosystem, to advance Spark, right? Because Spark was created in the Hadoop ecosystem. And these are the Hadoop companies, right? So this was in the first year or so. We had all these partnerships despite the fact that some of these companies we knew could become our competitors, right? Because helping them to deploy, manage, and sell Spark-based services. So, in some sense, Microsoft fits our approach of trying to strike as many partnerships with other organizations in the ecosystem, being aggressive, doing partnerships with others. Even though, again, in some cases it was not clear-cut whether they are going to compete with us or not. But growing the ecosystem and growing Spark, that was the priority. We even had at some point a partnership with Snowflake. It requires a lot of heavy lifting. So we always look for partnerships which are meaningful. And I think great negotiation, Ali and so forth did a fantastic job there. But at the end of the day, we also need to commit to it. It took tens of engineers one year to build Azure Databricks. We were on AWS before that.

items.question: Why were you willing to pursue aggressive partnerships at Databricks with companies that could compete with you?
items.object: Databricks’ strategy of partnering with potential competitors
items.answer: In general, this was our approach. We are going to be aggressive also about partnerships, even though the partners could compete and overlap, because you have to trust yourself that at least when it comes to Spark you can build the best products. items.question: How did you think about betting Databricks' success on Spark?
items.object: Databricks' decision to bet on Spark
items.answer: I mean, you try to simplify things. Initially we said, look, we have to make Spark win. I remember, look at all these combinations: Spark wins and the product fails, or Spark loses but we have a product which is successful, or both fail. No, that's not very interesting. Or both are successful, right? And we convinced ourselves that we need to bet on Spark to win because that's the most likely way also for the product to win. Again, for better or worse, sometimes there could be many ways to success, and in retrospect you cannot go back and try other alternatives. Maybe there are better alternatives at that point. But it's important to commit to one thing which hopefully is a reasonably good solution, a good path forward, right? Again, there are many paths to the peak. The most important is to commit to one which leads to the peak, right? It's not the shortest one or the easiest one, but it has to be one to get there, and to the highest peak. And that's how we said, okay, Spark has to win, and we have to build the best place for Spark. items.object: Choosing research problems
items.answer: I've always been trying to focus on the problem. items.question: What do you value about Berkeley's research environment as a place to discover important problems?
items.object: Berkeley's research culture and five-year labs
items.answer: I like to preface by saying that it's obviously also a lot of luck involved, and being at a place at Berkeley and having fantastic students and colleagues around you—you couldn't do without that, right? It's his or her merit probably more than mine. Especially at Berkeley, you get exposed not only to new ideas but willingness to take risk and get into new areas. In some sense, and this is what I like about Berkeley, if you look traditionally, Berkeley, among top schools, they are the first to open new areas. So they are always kind of more, a little bit trying to experiment. I really resonated with it. Then the other thing that happened is Berkeley has these labs, which are like five-year labs. Each lab has a vision, and it's a group of faculty coming together who believe in their vision, with their students, and try to make it happen over five years. This has a lot of great impact. These labs have a very strong relation with industry, connection. I remember from Google, first time we got it, and it was unheard by them because they were asking for $500,000 per year, for four years. But we got it. So now you have also this kind of very tight connection with the industry. It's a very good environment to seize the problems, to understand the problems.

items.question: How do you use secular trends to recognize research opportunities such as distributed in-memory data processing?
items.object: Secular trends and the opportunity for distributed in-memory data processing
items.answer: I try to think about trends, because trends are important, right? You have to be aligned with these secular trends. You need to bet on the right trends because these are things you cannot change, or it's very hard to change. So if you're not aligned, it's not good. And these trends actually, there are multiple trends, and the multiple trends kind of open gaps between them, and these are opportunities for problems. Like, for instance, big data. It was clear you have more and more data, and the amount of data people were collecting was just growing, right? Google had seen that years before and they built all the systems. But now everyone wanted to emulate that. We have all these Hadoop people coming to our retreats on these labs and we are friends with them. And we started to see problems, and then you try to use them. There are these groups of Michael Jordan's students which wanted to compete in this Netflix challenge. Netflix released some data and asked for people to provide recommendations, come up with recommendation to build recommendation algorithm systems, to beat their own recommendation. So they come to us: okay, it's a lot of data, what can we do about it? And we tell them to do, yes, Hadoop. But Hadoop was very slow. And then I put together something quickly to solve this problem in which the data was kept in memory. The other thing I've seen is about a previous company, Conviva, an analytics company. It was very slow and we tried to do it for ad hoc queries, and there was no way to do it. Again, keeping the data in memory was a solution. So that's kind of how we started. On one hand, you have more and more data, growing faster than Moore's Law, so it's not going to fit on one machine and therefore you need to use multiple machines. And the only other question is, are the important datasets going to fit in memory, right? That's kind of the first question. And they are, because when people were doing our queries, you notice that when you look at the data from different Hadoop clusters from Yahoo and Microsoft and others, in a lot of cases when you do queries and analytics, you're not doing it on all the data. You do it for the most recent data. You want to see what happens yesterday, what happens last week, something like that. Once you get that, you have a lot of cases where that data is fitting in memory, and memory is still growing quite quickly. At that time, you connect the dots. And then it's about solving the problem. You have to focus on the problem, and you have to focus on the trends. The way they are connected, you want to solve a problem ideally which is going to be more important tomorrow than today.

items.question: Why do you see building systems that other people use as valuable academic research?
items.object: Building systems that other people use as an academic research method
items.answer: I'm talking about academia and industry because some people in academia push back and say, you know, there's a lot of engineering here. This is not what you should be doing in academia. But one thing I've always found is very satisfying: if you build a system in a new area, and that system is used by other people, then you are in the best position to understand the new problems in that area. Because people are going to use your system in different ways, and then you understand that. And going back, if you know the problem, you are also in a good position to solve it. So actually it directly helps you with your research, to be ahead. Because otherwise, where are you finding the problems? Of course, there are very good problems in theory which are not solved for decades and so forth. But other things people do: they go to Google and Microsoft and so forth, spend time to understand what is the problem they have, because to solve it. But that's a little bit unsatisfying, because you go to someone to learn about their problems. But the question is, why don't people solve those problems? Maybe they don't solve the problems because maybe they are not as important at a given time, and maybe for the right reasons they are too much in the future.

items.question: Why do you think we need to rethink most of the software stack for AI applications?
items.object: Rethinking the software stack for AI applications
items.answer: Right now, we need to rethink most of the software stack. Because, again, going back to the trends, the demands of these applications, in particular AI applications and so forth, are growing much quicker than the capabilities of a single processor, a single node, even if you consider accelerators. On the other hand, the infrastructure becomes much more complex. You need to run that application not only on one node, but on many nodes. It's distributed. But it's not only that; it's becoming very heterogeneous. In order to bridge a gap between the demand and capabilities of hardware, people build accelerators. That's why Nvidia is a trillion-dollar company, right? But now the infrastructure becomes even more complex. It's not only distributed; it's heterogeneous. When we started Spark, it was homogeneous. All the nodes are the same: some storage, some CPUs, that's all. But right now, look at the heterogeneity. You have Nvidia, and you have many others. You have TPUs from Google. Every cloud is having their own chip. Now you have AMD and Intel saying that everything is about AI, right? So now you have a huge gap between these applications and this very complex infrastructure, just growing in complexity. And then it's not only about CPU, the compute; it's about networking. You have InfiniBand and all of this RDMA and so forth, right? Huge heterogeneity. And the software stack has to abstract away that complexity for the developers. There is no way around. You want a single machine, or you have this operating system to abstract away the complexity, right? That's what makes it easy, right?

items.question: How do you think AI applications can cross the gap from human assistance to autonomy?
items.object: The transition from human-assisted LLM applications to autonomous AI systems
items.answer: I think the other one is about building applications, the compound AI you were talking about. Right now, these AI applications, in particular large language models, everyone is talking about large language models. The applications are like assistants for humans, right? Humans are in the loop. If you are thinking about customer support, if you are talking about copilot, if you are thinking about Q&A, question and answering, even summarization, you have a human helping a human to be much more productive, which is a fantastic application. But they cannot be autonomous. They are not yet autonomous. And to go from having the human in the loop to being autonomous is a huge gap, right? Because with autonomy, to have something autonomous, you need to have something which is running more deterministically. It's more reliable, right? Far more accurate, right? You need to get there because if you don't get there, you are still limited to having the system where there's a human in the loop. And the human becomes a bottleneck. It's just a certain number of people on the planet. And I think a lot of work will be about how to make our systems, at least some aspects of these large language model applications, more like an engineering discipline, where you can build much easier systems from smaller components.

items.question: How do you view the current partnership between academia, government, and industry in AI research?
items.object: The partnership between academia, government, and industry in AI research
items.answer: It's challenging. It's very challenging. When I came to the United States, I came to do my PhD, and I graduated from Carnegie Mellon University. I'm originally from Romania. One thing people admired about the United States is how well this collaboration and partnership, this three-way partnership between academia and government and industry, are working, right? Prime examples at that time was obviously the internet, which was a DARPA project, and of course academia had a huge impact. And also industry, it was whatever, the third industrial revolution people were saying. When it comes to AI today, that kind of partnership is broken. Industries, every company is doing this research in silos. They don't talk to each other as much. Academia, like you said, doesn't have resources. And the government doesn't invest as much. So I think that's something to be very concerned about. That's why I'm also a big proponent of open-source models. The U.S. and California kind of will lose in the long term if this isn't fixed.

items.question: How do you think the gap in resources between academia and industry affects AI innovation?
items.object: The gap in AI research resources between academia and industry
items.answer: It's like OpenAI and Microsoft, they are talking about building the data centers about $100 billion, right? And I think the danger is that some of the academics are going to give up and try to innovate around the edges. Now, you can still innovate in applications and things like that, and I think there's a lot of innovation there. But clearly it's going to be harder to come up with newer model architectures and innovate. It will be harder. It's not impossible. Nothing is impossible. So yes, it's a challenge right now. There are people who are in a bit more fortunate position, maybe I'm one of them, who have access to resources outside academia. But you do want to level the playing field in order to maximize the innovation. The innovation comes from everywhere. Now, this being said, it's true that scarcity, and always in the past scarcity, spurs innovation. items.question: How do you see model distillation shaping the role of larger foundation models?
items.object: Model distillation and the continued development of larger foundation models
items.answer: I think people will continue to build larger models. I think that when it comes to serving, it looks like model distillation works quite well. By the way, model distillation is where you train a smaller model on the outputs from the bigger model. This has been a lot of success with that. By the way, in some way it shows how important the data is for training a model, right? Because you have higher-quality data from the big model and you use that to train the small model, and it's working very well. So I think using multiple distillation models to reduce the cost of inference is going to be a way forward. But yes, I think for advancing and pushing the frontiers, so to speak, pun intended, you are still going to see a lot of effort on bigger models.

items.question: How do you think founders should approach building an AI application amid the hype?
items.object: Building an AI application startup
items.answer: I would say it's the same thing: focus on the problem. Don't focus on the hype. The hype is emotional. It's not reliable. Just look at the facts, right? Look at the problem. Try to understand the problem and try to be truthful to yourself. And if you build an application, it's about production. It's not about the demo. It's beyond the demo. Of course, the demos are important. Don't get me wrong. They're very important. But production is the mindset you have to have. And, yeah, a dangerous thing is that there's so much hype, and you think you can solve everything and you can do everything. Probably in a certain number of years, but now just focus on exactly what problems you are going to solve. Convince yourself it's a good problem. Convince yourself that you can solve it, or at least you can have an MVP, right? You can solve a smaller version of that problem, which is still very valuable for your customers. That's what I would say.
